messages.subject: genome scan adjustment
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl, dear all,

in our study in mouse we are interested in genetic control of placenta weight from chromosome X. The belief that the genetic control is located on chromosome X is based on PREVIOUS studies of DIFFERENT authors. In our study ONLY chromosome X was genotyped.

Am I right to claim, that when computing significance threshold, it is necassary to adjust for a whole-genome scan which was (perhaps) performed by ohter authors many years ago? In practice, it means that
the X-chromosome specific false positive rate \alpha_X has to be modified the following way:

\alpha_X = 1-(1-\alpha)^{L_X/L} ,

where L is the genetic length of whole mouse genome amd L_X is genetic length of
chromosome X.

For adjusted p-value it holds:

p_X = 1-(1-p)^{L/L_X}.

In practice for L_X/L = 1/17 (in mouse) it means
\alpha_X=0.003 instead of unadjusted \alpha_X=0.05 and for example
instead of unadjusted p-value p=0.05 the adjusted one p_X=0.58.

Is it necassary to make such an adjustment?

I really appreciate your help.

Vaclav

messages.subject: Heterozygotes and QTLs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

I have a RIL population that has fairly messy data. For some reason, there is a large percentage of heterozygous genotypes for the generation of the individuals (~20%). After much manual curation of the data, i've been able to construct a genetic map using the physical positions as a reference for marker order. This has left me with a handful of markers in good agreement using maximum likelihood, regression mapping and physical positions.

My first question is, i if want to read the data as a backcross (which obviously gives me a warning for having too many genotype classes) and use convert2riself and omit all of those heterozygotes, then use mqmaugment or sim.geno to impute them, what would be the implications in terms of my QTL detections for MQM (or any any analysis)?

My second question is, what are the implications of eliminating identical/problematic individuals for map construction and then restoring the excluded ones for qtl analysis in the effort to have more phenotypic data (my population size is small)?

Thank you,

Valerio

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Kruskal-Wallis
messages.body_plain:
The nonparametric statistic in scanone is basically Kruskal-Wallis, but dealing with missing genotype information. See Broman (2003) Genetics 163:1169-1175 http://bit.ly/2partPDF

It's not implemented for composite interval mapping (or scantwo, for that matter). I'm not aware of such a nonparametric statistic that can handle covariates or multiple loci.

You could try converting the phenotype to normal scores (turn into ranks and then calculate the corresponding normal quantiles); use the function nqrank() in R/qtl. That tends to behave similarly to the non-parametric methods.

karl
